extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, media students and researchers interested in television/news-satire programming
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of production, stylistic, and editorial criteria embodied by Last Week Tonight with John Oliver — how episodes are structured, what comedic and informational standards the show follows, and strategies it uses for audience engagement and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main segment: one issue in depth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each episode's main segment covers one political or social issue in length, even if it may not have received recent news coverage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The show typically dedicates the substantial portion of an episode to a single topic, allowing extended exposition and analysis; occasionally the main segment can occupy the entire episode. Shorter segments usually cover recent news, while the main piece is a deep dive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy styles used
rubrics_metrics.description: "Alongside satire, the show uses self-referential humor, black comedy and observational comedy, and has been noted for its informative and fact-based content."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend multiple comedic modes (satire, self-referential jokes, black comedy, observational humor) while grounding content in facts to inform as well as entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode structure: short segments + main segment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each episode contains a small handful of shorter segments and then one main segment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorter topical items to open or punctuate the show and reserve the longer main segment for an in-depth examination of a systemic issue; sometimes short segments are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing via produced comedy elements (commercial-break function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers: "we are constructing these little, produced comedy elements that will serve the function of commercial breaks throughout the show, which will let us get out of the studio, get us away from John's voice and break the show up a bit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert produced bits, sketches, or filmed segments to vary pace and avoid sustained monologue fatigue; treat them like non-commercial 'breaks' that refresh the viewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parody-correspondent approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver: "we're not going to be a parody news show, so no people pretending to be journalists."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on actor-correspondents acting as faux journalists; the show distinguishes itself from parody-news formats by using other devices rather than recurring fake-news reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of video compilations and full-screen sourced clips
rubrics_metrics.description: "Oliver's speech is broken up with video compilations of recent news clips... A full-screen graphic will show and play a video clip (such as excerpts from news show or documentaries) when Oliver is citing it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave curated news clips and documentary excerpts to support claims and provide evidence; use full-screen playback to foreground source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-screen panel graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show includes a panel in the upper-left corner that frequently displays a photo or graphic that accompanies the subject at hand, as a comedic aid."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ small persistent graphics (panels) for quick visual jokes or to annotate points without interrupting the main framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring mascots and characters
rubrics_metrics.description: "A recurring element of the show is Oliver's use of mascots. The mascots used in the show include Jeff the Diseased Lung in a Cowboy Hat, Hoots the NSA Owl, Taryn the Tinder Chicken, and the Last Week Tonight puppets."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and reuse mascots/characters as comedic anchors and campaignable artifacts; they can be leveraged for satire, merchandising, or call-to-action campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage social media and hashtags
rubrics_metrics.description: "He often coins hashtags related to his segment for use in social media, some of which go viral."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design segment-linked hashtags and social-media-friendly assets to encourage viral sharing and audience-driven amplification of topics covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest selection and use
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show frequently features one or more celebrity guests... Guests have featured in many different capacities including giving monologues directly to camera, being interviewed by Oliver, playing musical numbers, participating in comedic skits..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite guests who can advance the segment's narrative — celebrities, experts, or people directly involved in the issue — and deploy them in varied roles (interview, skit, monologue, PSA parody). HBO advised freedom 'not to feel obligated to feature celebrities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include first‑hand sources and on-location interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: "Oliver has interviewed personalities who were directly involved in or impacted by the issues being discussed... Oliver traveled to Moscow to interview Snowden, and traveled to Dharamsala, India to interview the 14th Dalai Lama."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, incorporate interviews with primary participants or eyewitnesses and conduct on-location reporting to add authority and perspective to a segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: deeper dives and systemic context
rubrics_metrics.description: "Last Week Tonight has taken a more specific approach to deeper dives into systemic issues which intend to illustrate both the wider socio-political context and the complex interconnections and embeddedness of public policies in social outcomes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to explain not just the surface events but the underlying systems, policy connections, and long-term implications to give audiences a broader contextual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection: watch widely and favor 'stories told badly' or 'off the grid'
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver: "I basically have to watch everything... I'm watching with a certain thing in mind and that is how to see a story told badly." "I think we'll be attracted to some extent by stories that are off the grid..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff should monitor a wide range of media to identify stories that are being misreported or neglected; favor international or undercovered topics when they offer stronger long-form narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy-first editorial stance but fact-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many media outlets have described Oliver's style as journalism or investigative journalism, "Oliver himself disagrees, stating that 'it's not journalism, it's comedy — it's comedy first, and it's comedy second.'" The show is also "noted for its informative and fact-based content."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize comedic effect while maintaining factual grounding; the program's dual identity requires balancing satire with verifiable evidence (which also mitigates legal risks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and digital strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The show posts segments to YouTube (main segment uploads schedule varied by season) and produces Web Exclusives; in 2024 the show began uploading full episodes in territories without local broadcast rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use online platforms and supplemental web-exclusive content to broaden reach; maintain a predictable upload schedule to maximize views and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stunts, demonstrations, and projects to illustrate or test points
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: creating 'Our Lady of Perpetual Exemption' to demonstrate how easy it is to set up a tax-exempt church; buying medical debt and forgiving it; launching mascots and marketing campaigns (Jeff the Diseased Lung); publishing a parody children's book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, employ real-world stunts, experiments, or creative projects that exemplify systemic problems or catalyze public engagement — but be prepared for legal, ethical, and journalistic scrutiny. Such actions have driven tangible public responses (the 'John Oliver Effect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Title sequence and tonal framing
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show's title sequence presents images relating to the world at large with satirical captions written in dog Latin (e.g., a photo of a gun labelled 'deus ex machina'...)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a stylized title sequence and recurring tonal cues to set satirical expectations and brand the show's voice before each episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible episode composition and follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: "On occasion, the short segments are omitted and the main segment takes up the entirety of the episode. Some episodes will follow up the main segment with another video compilation or news story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible with runtime and structure: allow the subject matter to dictate whether the episode includes multiple parts, a single long-form piece, or post-segment follow-ups.
